questions.stem: When you alter course or speed to avoid a collision, how large should the alteration be?
options: As small as possible, so you stay close to your planned track
Large enough for the other vessel to notice it, by eye or on radar
Exactly 10 degrees, as set out in the rule
Large enough to be seen by your own crew on the plotter
questions.explanation: The point of an avoiding action is that the other vessel can read it. The rule gives no fixed number of degrees, so the 10 degree option is wrong. What counts is how it looks from the other vessel, not on your own screen. Small alterations to protect a track defeat the purpose.

questions.stem: You are the give-way vessel and the range is closing. Which approach best matches Rule 8?
options: A series of small course changes, so you can watch how the other vessel responds
Wait until the vessels are very close, then make one large emergency turn
One early, clear alteration, then check that it is working
Hold your course and speed until the other vessel has acted
questions.explanation: Rule 8 asks for action that is positive and early, and discourages a succession of small alterations. Waiting until the last moment leaves little room to act, and holding on is the stand-on vessel's role, not the give-way vessel's.

questions.stem: With plenty of sea room, an alteration of course alone can be a very effective avoiding action. Which set of conditions does Rule 8 attach to that?
options: It must be made in good time, be substantial, and not create another close-quarters situation
It must always be to starboard, be at least 30 degrees, and be logged
It must be combined with a speed reduction and a sound signal
It must only be made once the other vessel has altered first
questions.explanation: The rule says a course change alone may be the best action provided it is timely, substantial and does not set up a new close-quarters situation. It does not fix a direction or a number of degrees, and it does not require a speed change, a signal or waiting for the other vessel.

questions.stem: You have altered course and the other vessel now appears to be passing clear. For how long should you keep checking that your action is effective?
options: Until the bearing has changed by a few degrees
Until the other vessel has sounded a signal
Until the other vessel is finally past and clear
Until the next scheduled position fix
questions.explanation: The rule says to keep checking the effectiveness of the action until the other vessel is finally past and clear. A bearing starting to change, or a convenient time on the watch, is not the test, and the other vessel is not required to make any signal.

questions.stem: You are the give-way vessel in a narrow inlet. The other vessel is closing, there is a rocky shore close on the side you would like to turn towards, and a third vessel is astern of you. Which action is most consistent with Rule 8?
options: Make a series of 5 degree turns towards the rocks to avoid the third vessel
Maintain course and speed because there is not enough room to alter
Slow down, or stop and reverse if needed, in good time to give yourself room to pass the other vessel safely
Sound five short blasts and hold your course and speed
questions.explanation: Rule 8 expressly allows a vessel to reduce speed or take way off when more time is needed, which is the natural tool when sea room is limited. Small turns are discouraged and here would also lead towards danger. A give-way vessel does not simply hold on, and the doubt signal does not replace taking action.

questions.stem: A vessel that the rules say must not impede the passage of another vessel finds itself approaching that vessel so that risk of collision exists. Which statement is correct?
options: Its duty not to impede ends once risk of collision exists
It must still act early to leave sea room, with full regard to what the other rules require
It should wait for the other vessel to act first, since the other vessel has priority
It is only required to sound a warning signal
questions.explanation: Rule 8 says that a vessel required not to impede is not relieved of that duty by getting close, and must take early action and have full regard to the other rules. Waiting, or sounding a signal alone, does not meet that. The other vessel also stays bound by the rules and must not take its priority as an excuse to stop looking.

questions.stem: If the circumstances of the case admit, what qualities does Rule 8 ask of any action taken to avoid collision?
options: Positive, made in ample time and with due regard to good seamanship
Cautious, made at the last moment and kept as small as possible
Announced on VHF first, then made once the other vessel agrees
Always a turn to starboard of at least 20 degrees
questions.explanation: Rule 8 asks for action that follows the other Steering and Sailing Rules and, if the circumstances admit, is positive, made in ample time and with due regard to good seamanship. Last-moment or small actions are what the rule warns against, a VHF agreement is not a condition in Rule 8, and Rule 8 sets no fixed direction or number of degrees.

questions.stem: A large vessel can safely navigate only within a narrow channel, and a small vessel that must not impede her is closing so that risk of collision exists. What does Rule 8 say about the large vessel?
options: She may hold her course and speed whatever happens, because the small vessel must not impede her
She remains fully obliged to comply with the Steering and Sailing Rules
She must always stop and let the small vessel clear
She is excused from keeping a lookout until the small vessel has cleared
questions.explanation: Rule 8 says the vessel whose passage is not to be impeded remains fully obliged to comply with the Rules when the two vessels are approaching so as to involve risk of collision. The small vessel's duty not to impede does not give the large vessel a licence to ignore the Rules, and nothing excuses either vessel from the lookout. Stopping may or may not be the right action; the rule does not require it in every case.
